section_1.title: Introduction: What is a Vector?
section_1.content: Define a vector not just as a list of numbers, but as a directed arrow representing a move in space (magnitude and direction). Contrast scalars (single values) with vectors (multi-dimensional components).
section_1.example: Visualizing a 'Player Character' on a 2D game map moving 3 units right and 2 units up, represented as vector [3, 2].

section_2.title: Vector Addition: The Head-to-Tail Rule
section_2.content: Explain vector addition geometrically. Demonstrate placing the tail of the second vector at the head of the first. Introduce the concept of the 'Resultant' vector.
section_2.example: A cat chasing a butterfly: Vector A is the cat's initial movement, Vector B is the butterfly's sudden turn. The resultant shows the cat's total displacement.

section_3.title: Scalar Multiplication: Scaling the Arrow
section_3.content: Explain how multiplying a vector by a scalar changes its length (stretching or shrinking) or reverses its direction (negative scalars).
section_3.example: A 'Zoom' function on a smartphone map: scaling the displacement vector [1, 1] by 3 results in [3, 3], effectively moving the view further away from the origin.

section_4.title: Basis Vectors: The Building Blocks
section_4.content: Introduce 'i' [1, 0] and 'j' [0, 1] as the foundation of the 2D coordinate system. Explain that any vector is just a linear combination of these basis vectors.
section_4.example: Using Lego bricks (basis) to build a wall; regardless of the shape, every complex structure (vector) is built from these standard unit blocks.

section_5.title: Application and Conclusion
section_5.content: Briefly connect vectors to modern applications like Computer Graphics (transforming shapes) and Physics (force vectors). Recap the core concepts: Magnitude, Direction, and Linear Combination.
section_5.example: A drone flight controller calculating wind resistance (Vector A) vs. motor thrust (Vector B) to maintain a steady hover.
